strengths: The paper addresses a worthwhile problem: predicting human cognitive responses under changing environmental feedback. Combining task-solving representations, evidence accumulation, and reinforcement learning is a promising methodological contribution.

The reported prediction improvements are meaningful. On the math task, numeric-input CogReact achieves MAPE 0.2703 versus 0.3052 for the strongest listed baseline, approximately an 11.4% relative reduction. The video-input variant also improves over baselines using the same input format.

The evaluation includes component ablations, comparisons with neural models augmented with DDM, individual and leave-one-participant-out evaluations, and extensions to gambling and learning tasks. This breadth provides useful evidence of practical applicability.

The collection of 21,157 behavioral responses under four feedback schedules is a potentially valuable resource. The manuscript provides substantial implementation and experimental documentation and a code/data repository link.
weaknesses: The central mechanistic interpretation is insufficiently supported. Appendix A.7 constructs a noisy sigmoid trajectory from SVR-predicted response time and SVC confidence, without establishing its correspondence to a specified diffusion decision process. Training rewards only terminal response-time accuracy, so many different action trajectories can explain the same observation. Figure 3 therefore does not establish that the inferred trajectories recover human cognitive dynamics. Nonzero 'time-pressure effects' in the no-pressure group further illustrate possible conflation of stimulus effects with baseline prediction errors.

The experiments do not isolate the claimed benefit of fine-grained temporal stimulus modeling. The visual stimulus follows a fixed repeating timer, while the experimental conditions primarily vary its presence across trials. The stronger numeric-input result also leaves the necessity of detailed visual dynamics unresolved. Matched controls that remove or alter temporal information, and evaluation on unseen intervention schedules, would strengthen this principal claim. Leave-one-participant-out evaluation addresses a different generalization question.

The main DDM ablation changes several factors simultaneously: the pure DRL agent uses whole-video features, a different visual encoder, different action scaling, and a different episode horizon. Consequently, its accuracy and training-time disadvantages cannot be attributed specifically to removing DDM. Figure 11 provides a useful additional comparison, but matched supervised residual predictors and fitted cognitive models with time-varying drift or boundaries would better establish the contribution relative to relevant prior approaches.

The additional datasets raise unresolved validity questions. Appendix A.11 describes using alternative-outcome feedback to predict CPC18 response times; if this is the same trial's post-choice feedback, it was unavailable during the modeled decision. The temporal alignment needs clarification. For PeerEdu, the mapping from threshold-crossing dynamics to continuous curiosity is insufficiently explained, and MAPE on a target bounded between zero and one can be unstable near zero. Complementary absolute-error metrics are needed.

The statistical evidence is weaker than the reported significance suggests. Table 4 labels the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of individual prediction errors as a confidence interval; these do not quantify uncertainty in mean performance or model differences. The permutation procedures do not specify how participant clustering and paired predictions are handled, despite repeated observations per participant. Variability across training seeds is also not reported.

Important reproduction details remain unspecified, including the sigmoid and Brownian-noise parameterization, the perturbation coefficient lambda, and how the SVM stages are fitted within evaluation folds using the intended no-feedback data. The numeric-input and curiosity adaptations need explicit update equations. A smaller reporting inconsistency is the participant count: Section 3.1 reports 44, Table 2 lists 50, and Appendix A.3.1 identifies 36 retained participants.
